title: Golf: Who Gets to Play?
narrativeQuestion: Which barriers most shaped who could participate in golf, and how did they change?

chapters.title: The government wanted them practicing archery.
chapters.claim: A law banning a game proves people already knew it. It does not tell us who invented it.

chapters.title: The ground helped write the game.
chapters.claim: A sport grows differently when its playing surface is coastal land rather than a court with fixed measurements.

chapters.title: Eighteen holes was a choice.
chapters.claim: Rules and standards develop through decisions. They are not natural laws.

chapters.title: A better ball changes more than a score.
chapters.claim: Technology can change the cost of entry, the work of making equipment, and the land a sport needs.

chapters.title: The champion also had a job.
chapters.claim: Early professionals often earned their living through several kinds of golf work.

chapters.title: A traveling game brings institutions with it.
chapters.claim: Golf spread through people, travel, clubs, and governing organizations. Its expansion was uneven.

chapters.title: John Shippen belonged on that tee.
chapters.claim: An individual breakthrough can challenge exclusion while leaving larger barriers in place.

chapters.title: Read the patent, then check the story.
chapters.claim: An invention document supports specific claims. Popular stories often stretch those claims.

chapters.title: The former caddie beats the famous professionals.
chapters.claim: Francis Ouimet’s victory challenged expectations about who could become a champion.

chapters.title: Playing without prize money still takes resources.
chapters.claim: Amateur status and economic access are different questions.

chapters.title: The players helped build their own tour.
chapters.claim: Women’s professional golf required organizing work as well as strong performances.

chapters.title: Permission is only one part of access.
chapters.claim: Rules, money, travel, treatment, and ownership can each create a separate barrier.

chapters.title: A camera changes who sees the sport.
chapters.claim: Media can increase attention and revenue without giving every viewer a place to play.

chapters.title: One tournament has its own timeline.
chapters.claim: Lee Elder’s entry and Tiger Woods’s win were different milestones in different years.

chapters.title: Se Ri Pak changes the picture.
chapters.claim: International success grows through role models and the systems that help players follow them.

chapters.title: The course keeps working after the cameras leave.
chapters.claim: Everyday access depends on prices, location, public decisions, and paid work.

chapters.title: A green course has a resource bill.
chapters.claim: Environmental decisions need local evidence and visible tradeoffs.

chapters.title: Who gets to decide what golf becomes?
chapters.claim: Modern disputes return to older questions about work, control, money, and access.

accuracyNotes: Earliest surviving mention is not an invention date.
Written rules and the spread of the 18-hole standard are separate processes.
PGA of America, tours, clubs and tournaments have distinct access histories.
All model quantities are invented and clearly labeled.
1930 Grand Slam names its historical events, not the modern professional majors.
Later portraits carry dates and are not presented as event photographs.
The 2022–2023 business chapter makes no current-status claim.
Readonly activity records are learning evidence, not tamper-proof proof of authorship.
